title: Multi-hop tail latency investigation - Bifrost Energy technical deep dive
topics: VPC peering and multi-region network hops
summary: Short technical deep dive to triage Bifrost's observed p99 spikes on inference. Team walked through the request path (client -> VPC peering -> edge -> regional inference -> fallback model), discussed streaming vs non-streaming behavior, KV cache hotkeying, and batching impacts. Action items: run synthetic p99 multi-hop tests, share network topology and firewall rules, and provide quantization/batching recommendations and a draft Dedicated capacity baseline.
next_steps: Redwood to run multi-hop p99 test with 2k concurrent streams and share logs
Bifrost to provide network topology + firewall egress rules
Sofia to send Dedicated + Private deployment baseline and pricing
action_items: Sofia Patel: Send Dedicated/Private baseline + rough pricing by 2026-03-09
Daniel Ortega: Run multi-hop p99 benchmark (streaming + non-streaming) and upload logs by 2026-03-10
Evan Shaw: Share VPC subnet map, NAT/GW hop counts, and firewall rules by 2026-03-08
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-05
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Priya (Bifrost Head of ML), Evan (Infra), Marta (SRE)

[00:00] Sofia Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick agenda — triage the p99 spikes you saw in last week's run, talk through multi-hop implications, and agree next steps.
[00:12] Priya Kumar: Yep thanks. We've been seeing intermittent p99s up to 850ms on some flows, normal p95 around 120. It's mostly during batch-of-concurrent inference from our edge gateways.
[00:25] Daniel Ortega: Got it. Can you remind us the path — are these native streaming requests or single-chunk non-streamed responses?
[00:34] Evan Shaw: Mostly streaming from the edge to our aggregator service, then we call Redwood hosted inference in us-west-2 via VPC peering. Some traffic falls back to a cross-region replica in eu-west-1.
[00:48] Marta Ionescu: There's also a NAT in front which does some SNAT — could be adding a hop.
[00:55] Daniel Ortega: Ok important. Streaming vs non-streaming changes kernel utilization and latency tails. Streaming keeps the request open which can amplify network hop jitter. For p99 that often exposes hiccups in the KV cache warm path or a long tail on batching cutover.
[01:18] Priya Kumar: When you say KV cache warm path, are you referring to prefix cache misses or the KV shard rebalancing?
[01:25] Daniel Ortega: Both can matter. If you have hot-keys concentrated on a small subset and one of the KV shards is under pressure or gets temporarily evicted, p99 can spike — especially with streaming because the client holds the connection while the runtime retrieves KV entries.
[01:40] Evan Shaw: We do see a few very hot prompts — around 12% of requests. We suspected hot-keys but the infra team hasn't confirmed shard imbalances.
[01:52] Sofia Patel: Another vector is network multi-hop. If your VPC peering path crosses a transit gateway or a third-party firewall, each additional hop adds jitter and queuing. p95 vs p99 diverges fast with even 2–3 extra hops.
[02:08] Marta Ionescu: Sounds plausible — our peering goes through a shared transit gw in another account for routing.
[02:14] Daniel Ortega: Can you share the exact hop count and whether there's any per-connection state (like TLS termination or proxy) that could be reusing connections?
[02:24] Evan Shaw: We'll pull a topology. Quick question — how different are streaming and non-streaming tails from Redwood's perspective?
[02:31] Daniel Ortega: Streaming reads can show higher CPU per active connection because of continuous generator callbacks and buffer churn. Non-streaming (request/response) batches are more amenable to aggressive batching and can reduce p99 if you can tolerate the initial latency. But if you enable server-side batching, occasional batch formation delays create spikes for the first request in the batch.
[02:55] Priya Kumar: So tradeoff — streaming reduces TTFB for tokens but might increase p99 if network jitter or KV misses happen; non-streaming can have a higher median but tighter tail?
[03:04] Daniel Ortega: Exactly. Also quantization plays a role — int8 or q4_0 can reduce compute time, lowering median and tail on the model compute side, but it can increase variance if kernels fall back to slower code paths for particular sequence lengths or attention patterns.
[03:20] Sofia Patel: We should look at where the p99 is coming from — network vs runtime vs model compute. We'll want a waterfall breakdown: client-to-edge, edge-to-redwood ingress, scheduling/batching, model compute, KV lookups, and egress.
[03:36] Priya Kumar: We tried instrumenting some spans but our tracing sampling was set low. We'll increase trace sampling for the next test.
[03:43] Daniel Ortega: Great. For the test I propose: synthetic workload with 2k concurrent streams, mix of hot-keyed prompts and long context prompts, run both streaming and non-streaming, gather per-component timings and kernel traces if possible.
[03:58] Evan Shaw: Does Redwood provide a test harness for that?
[04:01] Daniel Ortega: We have an internal runner we can share — it's a script + config that hits hosted endpoints with controlled concurrency and reports p50/p95/p99, and also uploads raw request/response logs. We'll sanitize logs before upload.
[04:14] Priya Kumar: Okay send that over. Also can you comment on Dedicated — would moving to Dedicated reduce p99?
[04:21] Sofia Patel: Dedicated helps because you get reserved GPU pools and predictable scheduling latency; you'd remove noisy neighbors and potentially reduce scheduling jitter. But network hops still matter if the VPC path isn't simplified. If you go Private with a co-located inference node in your VPC, you can eliminate the peering hop altogether.
[04:37] Marta Ionescu: We were considering Private with an on-prem option for some regs. Any notes about on-prem quantization differences?
[04:44] Daniel Ortega: On-prem tends to have more predictable network but depends on hardware. Quantization efficacy is tied to kernel paths and CUDA/cuBLAS versions; we publish recommended quantization profiles per hardware family. Some older GPUs show worse tail variance with certain int8 kernels.
[04:58] Priya Kumar: For hot-keys — is there an approach to route certain prompts through a cached path?
[05:05] Daniel Ortega: Yes, prefix caching and explicit hot-key pinning are options. We can pin KVs to particular shards, and you can reserve an L1 prefix cache on the runtime for the few thousand hottest keys to reduce misses. Also a lightweight local edge cache is sometimes helpful to offload the first token.
[05:21] Evan Shaw: If we pin to shards, does that risk imbalance?
[05:24] Daniel Ortega: There's always tradeoffs — pinning reduces miss rate for hot keys but if the key distribution changes, you need to rebalance. We recommend autoscaling KV shards and monitoring key cardinality.
[05:36] Sofia Patel: To prioritize, let's get the network topology and run your multi-hop synthetic tests. Daniel will run the runner and we'll correlate.
[05:44] Priya Kumar: Sounds good. Specific question — we saw p99 spikes only in the evening batch windows when we had more cross-region fallbacks. Could cross-region fallbacks be the main culprit?
[05:55] Daniel Ortega: Very likely. Cross-region introduces higher base RTT and more variability. Also if the fallback model is a smaller variant with a different quant profile, the compute phase timing changes, which shows up in the tail.
[06:10] Marta Ionescu: We have some firewall rules that throttle long-lived connections — could that interact with streaming?
[06:15] Daniel Ortega: Yes, firewall idle timeouts and per-connection rate limiting can cut or stall streams which produce weird tails. Please include those rules in the topology doc.
[06:25] Evan Shaw: We'll include NAT rules and the transit gateway layout.
[06:29] Sofia Patel: On batching: if you enable adaptive batching, do we get better p99?
[06:33] Daniel Ortega: Adaptive batching targets throughput while respecting latency SLOs — it can help overall cost and median, but p99 depends on the batch cut heuristic. If the heuristic accidentally accumulates a large batch under certain traffic patterns, first-in-batch latency suffers. We typically set a max batch wait of 8–12ms for low-latency configs.
[06:50] Priya Kumar: And what about the runtime's kernel selection? Could sudden sequences trigger a fallback to generic kernels?
[06:56] Daniel Ortega: Yes — if you have long sequences or unusual attention patterns the runtime might pick a less-optimized kernel path. That shows up as infrequent but large spikes. We'll request kernel trace logs for the test runs.
[07:08] Evan Shaw: Is there anything we should change client-side quick to reduce p99 while we run tests?
[07:12] Daniel Ortega: A couple quick experiments: increase connection reuse (keep-alives), try toggling streaming off for a sample cohort, and reduce cross-region fallback by pinning a regional primary for a short window.
[07:24] Sofia Patel: I'll scope those client experiments in the next steps doc.
[07:28] Priya Kumar: On quantization — do you have benchmarks showing p99 improvements vs any regressions?
[07:34] Daniel Ortega: We do. Int8 tends to give a 20–40% median improvement, p99 improves in many cases, but some sequence-length edge cases can show 5–10% worse tail due to fallback code paths. We'll share the quant profiles specific to the model family and hardware.
[07:49] Marta Ionescu: If we move to Dedicated, is there an easy way to simulate Dedicated-like scheduling on hosted to test effect?
[07:56] Daniel Ortega: We can reserve capacity on your account for a short pilot (burst reservation) to approximate Dedicated behavior. It won't be identical but helps isolate scheduling noise.
[08:04] Evan Shaw: That would be useful.
[08:07] Sofia Patel: Action items recap in a bit. Any more deep diagnostics ideas?
[08:12] Daniel Ortega: One more — sample RT logs with timestamps and add jitter buckets. When you see a p99 at 850ms, break down the request into: TLS handshake (should be negligible), network RTT, scheduling wait, KV lookup, model compute, and token forwarding. If we can get those spans at 1ms granularity we'll be in good shape.
[08:30] Priya Kumar: We'll increase trace sampling.
[08:33] Daniel Ortega: Also instrument kernel counters — like the kernel selection id and quant path indicator — that'll tell us if a fallback happened.
[08:42] Evan Shaw: Performance wise, is there a rule of thumb for when to enable local edge caching vs. rely on Redwood's prefix cache?
[08:49] Daniel Ortega: If your hot-key hit ratio >5% and latency budget is <200ms, local edge cache is recommended. If hit ratio is lower, rely on runtime prefix caching which is more cost-effective.
[09:04] Sofia Patel: Ok let's do a quick timeline: Redwood runs multi-hop test by Tuesday (Daniel), Bifrost sends topology by Sunday (Evan), Redwood shares quant profiles and Dedicated pilot options by Monday (Sofia). Anything else?
[09:17] Priya Kumar: Please also send us a short doc explaining streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs for our product managers.
[09:22] Sofia Patel: Will do.
[09:25] [rough cross-talk, notes exchanged]
[09:40] Daniel Ortega: Technical nit — when you run the runner, please enable two modes: "streaming-keepalive" and "nonstream-batched". Use the same request distribution and vary concurrency. Capture kernel traces and raw latency histograms.
[09:55] Evan Shaw: Understood. One last question — do you have any automated alerts that correlate network anomalies with p99 spikes?
[10:02] Daniel Ortega: In Console you can set p99 alerting and correlate with infra traces and connection errors. We also recommend exporting system metrics into your APM to do joint spiking correlation.
[10:15] Marta Ionescu: We'll set up an alert to flag when p99 crosses 500ms for more than 5 minutes.
[10:20] Sofia Patel: Great. Quick recap and next steps — Daniel will run the runner and share results (multi-hop streaming + non-streaming); Evan provides topology and firewall/NAT rules; Sofia shares Dedicated/Private baseline, quant profiles, and a short PM-facing streaming vs non-streaming note.
[10:38] Priya Kumar: Thanks everyone, appreciate the time.
[10:42] Sofia Patel: Thanks — we'll follow up in Slack and send the artifacts.
[10:45] [meeting ends]
